issues.title: How do we do secure channel to RA binding?
issues.author: ionut-arm
issues.body:
This issue comes up a lot, including during the presentation at IETF-124 and on the mailing list. I'll define in words for now what we mean by cryptographic binding, why we think we need it, how it can be achieved.

## Summary

Cryptographic binding between a secure channel (establishment) session and a remote attestation session gives the attester's peer (calling them relying party or RP henceforth) confidence that the secure channel endpoint is the attester. So if the attester has a WebPKI-based identifier, the RP can also trust that the attestation credential (AC) is representative of the entity who owns that identifier.

**Attacker model**: The strongest attacker I can think of is a service provider who wants to pretend that their service resides in a TEE (or another attested environment). They have access to webPKI certs and the associated key material. They can also control the routing of traffic to this service, and can spin up the workloads they want to impersonate in attestable environments. Their only difficulty is in convincing the RP that the AC and the CertificateVerify are coming from the same endpoint.

## Why?

Strong binding is needed to prevent a malicious "attester" from just conveying an AC taken from a legitimate TEE as its own - in other words, to prevent a Man in the Middle. Without some sort of binding, the provenance of the AC can't be established, and so the RP should not trust its contents. For example, relying strictly on nonces for this would not be sufficient, since the nonces can just be forwarded to/from separate sessions.

## How?

This is the crux of the problem and I'm not sure whether we should describe any specific mechanism in this draft, but instead leave it to protocol designers to ensure MitM is not possible.

Nevertheless, here are some examples of how to achieve this in the context of TLS in particular:

* Export some keying material from the TLS session and include it in the AC. The RP can verify this binding to confirm the provenance. **Pro**: strong guarantee. **Con**: more complex to implement (?), perhaps going as far as making changes to key schedule.
* Bind the AC to the attester's webPKI cert (e.g., by hashing the cert, or the public key...). The RP can verify that the AC was issued for an entity who owns that cert, which CertificateVerify proves is the peer. **Pro**: simpler to implement and does not involve invasive changes to secure channel protocol. **Con**: this only works if the webPKI-certified key has never left the TEE / attester; if it was provisioned at runtime, the guarantee vanishes (since the key owner could just use the same webPKI credential from an insecure context).
* Bind the webPKI cert to the (unique) attesting platform. The RP can verify that the platform identifier from the webPKI cert corresponds to whatever is in the AC. **Pro**: similar to above. **Con**: Similar to above, plus it's only possible if the attester has a unique identity.

Maybe these last two options also point to a tiered approach: you can either do direct binding to session, or binding through webPKI cert AND a new property that the certified key has never left / cannot leave the attester.

## Questions for WG

* At what level of detail do we describe it in the draft?
    * Does it limit the scope of the charter if we go with a lower-level wording?
* Do we need to perhaps phrase it as a negative property instead? e.g. "Protocol is not subject to MitM of AC"

comments.author: tireddy2
comments.body:
In our draft, the attestation evidence or attestation results are carried inside the Certificate message. The CertificateVerify signature also covers the Handshake Context defined in RFC 9261, which is derived from exporter-secret–based values taken from the TLS session. This means the signature is bound both to the webPKI certificate and to the TLS session in which the authenticator is generated. Only the entity that holds the private key corresponding to the webPKI certificate and that has access to the exporter-secret of the session can produce a valid CertificateVerify.

However, the binding described above does not by itself prevent a server from obtaining attestation evidence from a different TEE and presenting it as its own. A malicious server that legitimately holds the webPKI  certificate private key and controls the TLS session can export the session-specific exporter values and forward them to a remote TEE, which can in turn produce attestation evidence that verifies correctly inside the Certificate message. To ensure that the attestation evidence originates from the same environment that holds the certificate private key, the attestation evidence will have to include the public key of the webPKI certificate used in the Certificate message, together with claims that the corresponding private key is generated and protected within the TEE.

issues.title: Add a new operation-triggered use case of attested TLS
issues.author: Yuning-J
issues.body:
Hi,

I propose the following operation-triggered use case of attested TLS, to be added into your existing use case draft [here](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-mihalcea-seat-use-cases/):

----------------------------------------------------
3.4. Operation-Triggered Attestation for High-Impact Application Operations

Goal: Ensure the integrity of application services at operation time, when security posture may change after initial channel establishment.

Use case: High-Assurance Operation Execution in Dynamic Application Services: An application service instance (e.g., AI agent) or confidential computing environment (which could host an AI agent) maintains a (D)TLS connection with a peer and must execute a high-impact action (e.g., payment initiation, configuration change, privileged command).

Requirement 1: Before executing a high-impact operation over the existing connection, the peer must presents fresh, connection-bound attestation evidence reflecting the current behavior-affecting posture (e.g., enabled capabilities, policy configuration, runtime permissions). 

Requirement 2: The mechanism SHOULD support lightweight, dynamic attestation within the existing connection, without necessarily requiring a full new TLS handshake, so that behavior-affecting posture changes are visible to relying parties when required by local policy.

----------------------------------------------------

Any comment and feedback are welcome to refine the descriptions.

/Yuning

issues.title: Analyze the role of attester/RP in each use case
issues.author: Yuning-J
issues.body:
Hi team,

I performed an analysis mapping the attester role(s) and VRP for each use case. This is based on the draft's descriptions, inferred TLS client/server roles (e.g., who initiates connections and needs proof), and RATS terminology (RFC 9334).

I'd love feedback from the authors on whether this mapping aligns with your intent, or if clarifications/additions to the draft would help (e.g., adding explicit roles).

3.1 Secure Provisioning and High-Assurance Operations 

3.1.1.Use case: Runtime Secret Provisioning. --> Require: Client as attester.
Reasoning: A confidential workload (TLS client) must prove its runtime state and TEE trustworthiness to a secrets management service (TLS server) before receiving sensitive secrets.

3.1.2.Use case: High-Assurance Command Execution --> Require: Server as attester.
Reasoning: An operator (TLS client) issues critical commands to a remote system (TLS server), but only after the system proves its integrity to avoid execution on a compromised device.

3.2 Confidential Data Collaboration

3.2.1.Use case: Data Clean Rooms. --> Require: Both (mutual attestation). **Could clarify if mutual is always required?**
Reasoning: Data providers (TLS clients) and consumers (TLS server) must each verify that a shared confidential workload runs authorized code in a secure TEE before sharing or processing data.

3.2.2.Use case: Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) --> Require: Both (mutual attestation).
Reasoning: Participating (TLS clients) and a central aggregator (TLS server) must all prove they are running the correct MPC algorithm in trusted environments to ensure privacy-preserving computation.

3.3 Network Infrastructure Integrity

3.3.1.Use case: Attestation of Network Functions. --> Require: **Both (mutual attestation)?**
Reasoning: The use case describes device integrity verification by the orchestrator, implying device as client/attester. However, in some management flows (e.g., orchestrator-initiated connections), roles might switch or require mutual attestation.

3.3.2.Use case: Securing Control and Management Planes --> Require: **NOT SURE?**
Reasoning: The use case has the admin client verifying the device, suggesting device as server/attester and admin as client/RP. Confirm if this holds, or if mutual attestation applies in some variants?

3.4 Operation-Triggered Attestation for High-Impact Application Operations

3.4.1.Use case: High-Assurance Operation Execution in Dynamic Application Services --> Require: Server as attester.
Reasoning: An application service instance (e.g., AI agent, acting as TLS server) must provide fresh, connection-bound attestation Evidence reflecting its current posture (e.g., capabilities, permissions) before executing high-impact actions over an existing connection with a peer (TLS client).

3.5 Trusted Software and Firmware Upgrade

3.5.1. Use case: Integrity Attestation During Software/Firmware Upgrade Deployment --> Require: Client as attester.
Reasoning: A network device (TLS client) must be verified by an orchestrator (TLS server) for a healthy baseline state before, during, and after upgrades, with verified rollback if needed.


Questions for feedback:
- Does this role mapping match your vision? Any adjustments?
- For ambiguous cases (marked with ?), should we add variants (e.g., mutual or role-switching) to the draft?

Thanks for your thoughts. This could help refine the draft and ensure better alignment with further implementations.

Best,  
Yuning

comments.author: Yuning-J
comments.body:
Building on the attester role mapping I shared above (client/server/mutual across the use cases), I've extended the analysis to consider whether each scenario is best addressed via **intra-handshake** (e.g., one-time verification at connection establishment), **post-handshake** (e.g., dynamic/fresh evidence over existing sessions without renegotiation), or a hybrid. This is inferred from the use cases' emphasis on timing, freshness, and dynamics (e.g., runtime checks or phased processes).

Not all use cases fit neatly into one category, some prioritize efficiency at setup (intra), while others need runtime updates (post). 

A fuller mapping is below for discussion:

| Use Case | Best Approach | Reasoning |
|----------|---------------|-----------|
| 3.1.1 Runtime Secret Provisioning | Hybrid (intra + post) | One-time attestation during initial setup, but could benefit from post for ongoing or refreshed secret management in long sessions. |
| 3.1.2 High-Assurance Command Execution | Post-handshake | Requires fresh evidence over potentially long-lived connections; avoids renegotiation for efficiency. |
| 3.2.1 Data Clean Rooms | Hybrid (intra + post) | Focus on pre-data-sharing verification, intra suffices for setup; post enables re-checks in long sessions or ongoing data flows. |
| 3.2.2 Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) | Intra-handshake | Mutual setup-phase attestation; no explicit runtime elements. |
| 3.3.1 Attestation of Network Functions | Intra-handshake | Tied to joining/onboarding; one-time baseline check. |
| 3.3.2 Securing Control and Management Planes | Intra-handshake | Verification at connection time to the management interface; initial trust focus. |
| 3.4.1 High-Assurance Operation Execution in Dynamic Application Services | Post-handshake | Explicit need for lightweight, dynamic attestation without full handshakes for posture changes. |
| 3.5.1 Integrity Attestation During Software/Firmware Upgrade Deployment | Hybrid (intra + post) | Initial baseline via intra; continuous pre/during/post verification benefits from post-handshake freshness. |

I'd appreciate input from the use case authors on this intra/post mapping—does it align with your scenarios? Any adjustments, or should we add explicit guidance in the draft on preferred mechanisms per use case?

Thanks!  
Yuning

comments.author: muhammad-usama-sardar
comments.body:
I like the approach but there are factual errors in this table, as pointed [here](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/seat/-hrVLla9pyWGrcTxzBvNkf6MfBY/). As the expat draft mentions, you should do post-handshake attestation round immediately after the handshake. Moreover, all use cases are covered by post-handshake attestation by doing a one-time attestation round just after handshake, as Microsoft, Google and SCONE are using it in all cases. 

Moreover, criteria for "Best" needs to be discussed. Seems to be making a lot of assumptions. Security seems completely ignored.

comments.author: ionut-arm
comments.body:
Hi @Yuning-J !

A few notes on the role analysis:

> 3.1.2.Use case: High-Assurance Command Execution

I think I'd agree with @yaronf on this one (#5), it felt a bit weird to begin with. The issue I see is that a compromised system doesn't really need an admin to send a command for it to do Bad Things ™️ , it can just do them, unless it needs some secret or sensitive value to begin with. This would turn the "high-assurance command execution" framing into another "secret provisioning" use-case, just that the secret provider is now the TLS client. Thoughts?

> 3.2.1.Use case: Data Clean Rooms. --> Require: Both (mutual attestation). Could clarify if mutual is always required?
> Reasoning: Data providers (TLS clients) and consumers (TLS server) must each verify that a shared confidential workload runs authorized code in a secure TEE before sharing or processing data.

For this use-case I had understood both data providers and consumers as TLS clients, with the clean room surfacing API endpoints for either of them. But this isn't really coming from some idiomatic pattern for structuring these deployments.
I don't know if "mutual attestation" would be needed here, since I don't think there's much of a reason for the data clean room to attest either providers or clients.

> 3.3.1.Use case: Attestation of Network Functions. --> Require: Both (mutual attestation)?
> Reasoning: The use case describes device integrity verification by the orchestrator, implying device as client/attester. However, in some management flows (e.g., orchestrator-initiated connections), roles might switch or require mutual attestation.

Can you expand on that need for mutual attestation here, I'm not sure I follow?
I do wonder whether this would be better understood as "client wishing to use network functions attesting their platform"?

Regarding intra/post/hybrid classification, I'm not entirely sure. It depends on details that I'm not familiar with, regarding how the connections for these operations are set up, how long they stay up etc. I've just raised #24 which would help me (and probably others in the community) make better sense of how we reached these conclusions!

The first idea was to label when the attestation is (first) needed, with regards to the establishment of the secure channel (i.e., do we need to attest before any data is sent over the channel, or is it only needed at specific times before you send over some sensitive data?). issues.title: Yaron's feedback
issues.author: muhammad-usama-sardar
issues.body:
[Archive link](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/seat/dcBddogh7LeoCLM0VFX9uZqLLhQ/)

> 
> At Tiru’s request, I reread version -01 of the draft, below are my comments.
> 
> In general I’m not very happy with the draft but I’m also not sure it matters, because as far as I know we are not planning to publish it as an RFC. Chairs, please correct me if I'm wrong.
> 
> The document is still made of two almost disconnected parts: use cases and requirements. But it’s totally unclear to me how to obtain specific protocol-level requirements from any of the use cases. So as it is, the document is IMHO not very helpful in building the protocol(s) that address the SEAT charter.
> 
> Detailed comments:
> 
> Secure Channel Protocols
> I'm not sure why the title and abstract discuss generic "secure channel protocols", I believe SEAT is only chartered for TLS. (Yes, the charter text is initially not terribly clear on this but the scoping is all about TLS.)
> 
> Internal State
> “Identity authentication provides no assurance about the peer's internal state or the integrity of its software stack." - I don't think attestation typically provides strong assurance about a peer's internal state, e.g. its volatile memory. It does provide information about some of the state (the less volatile parts) at a certain point in time.
> 
> Trusted Computing Base
> This is a very old, well defined term, so let's use an existing definition instead of making our own. RFC 4949: The totality of protection mechanisms within a computer system, including hardware, firmware, and software, the combination of which is responsible for enforcing a security policy.
> 
> The Use Cases Do Not Determine the Solution
> Most of the use cases are totally valid, but I don't think any of them mandates an attested TLS solution. I believe each of them can easily be implemented at the application level, given enough expertise.
> The motivation for attested TLS is to make it easier/cheaper to implement these use cases and similar ones even if you don't have the expertise. IMO this is a very good reason, but it's still a jump from the use cases to the proposed solution.
> With that in mind, I don't think the use cases directly lead to the "integration properties".
> 
> Cryptographic Binding to Machine Identifier
> This may be a valid requirement for some use cases, but not in general. The current text is "Evidence should be cryptographically bound to the identifier provided to the machine by the infrastructure provider". This assumes there is a separate infrastructure provider, which may not be the case. And if one exists (cloud environments), applications typically do not have access to (i.e., cannot validate) machine identities. Moreover, applications usually only care about the attested software stack and not the physical identity of a machine. So I’m sure there are some cases where this makes sense, but I think most deployments will not need it.
> 
> Thanks,
>       Yaron
>

issues.title: Ekr review of -02
issues.author: muhammad-usama-sardar
issues.body:
[Archive link](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/seat/D2mIlXUtKUgKUPZmwDfwqnd7wWU/)

> TL;DR. I think the WG probably should adopt this document. While
> imperfect, the WG has a charter item to produce a use cases document
> and this seems to be the only candidate after 7 months. Ordinarily I
> would prefer documents to be in better shape before adoption but as
> this is a use case document not a specification, I think it's probably
> OK.
> 
> With that said, I find myself unpersuaded by many of the use cases
> here, for a variety of reasons, including:
> 
> (1) It's not clear that they really work
> (2) They seem to exist to shore up otherwise bad practices
> (3) Better approaches are available
> 
> In addition, it seems like some of the text here is requirements for
> the use case (e.g., " The network orchestrator must verify the
> device's integrity (e.g., S 4.4 Req 1) and other text is about the
> solution (e.g., S 4.4 Req 2). This is confusing.
> 
> For these reasons, I think this document will need quite a bit of
> work.
> 
> 
> S 1.3.
> 
> >    This document is intended as an input to the design of protocol
> >    solutions within the SEAT working group.  It defines the "why" (the
> >    motivation) and the "what" (the requirements), but not the "how" (the
> >    protocol design itself).  The "how" part is discussed in the
> >    companion document [I-D.usama-seat-intra-vs-post], which serves as
> >    the glue between this document and the protocol specifications.  A
> 
> This text will need to be removed prior to adoption unless there
> is a contemporaneous or prior decision to adopt draft-usama.
> 
> 
> S 3.5.
> 
> >    Peers have a secure mechanism to discover each other's support for
> >    RA, the specific attestation formats they can produce or consume, and
> >    the attestation models they support.  This enables interoperability
> >    and allows for graceful fallback for endpoints that do not support
> >    RA.
> 
> 
> Why do we need to support multiple attestation formats?
> 
> 
> S 3.8
> 
> >    It should be possible for the Relying Party to request new Evidence
> >    periodically or on-demand during the lifetime of the connection.
> >    This may be necessary if the Target Environment has attributes that
> >    can change during the connection, thereby affecting its
> >    trustworthiness.  Such changes cannot be detected using Evidence
> >    collected earlier.  For example, the Evidence may include dynamic
> >    parameters such as runtime configuration flags (e.g., FIPS mode),
> >    which indicate whether the device has entered or exited an approved
> >    mode, or measurements of critical system files.
> 
> 
> As I indicated in the discussions that produced the charter, I don't
> think this provides adequate security guarantees. Consider the following
> sequence of events, in which the Server is attesting to the client.
> 
> - Server attests to being in configuration 1, which is acceptable
>   to the client.
> - Client sends secret S1 to the server.
> - Server changes to configuration 2, which is not acceptable to the
>   client.
> - Client sends secret S2 to the server.
> - Client forces server to re-attest, discovers that the configuration
>   is unacceptable, and terminates the connection.
> 
> Unfortunately, this doesn't help the client because it's already
> sent S1 and S2. Even if you assume that the server properly
> disposed of S1, the client sent a secret to S2.
> 
> The point here is that part of the attestation by the server not only
> that it is currently in an acceptable configuration but also that it
> will not adopt a new configuration except under certain conditions
> (e.g., that it will notify the client and receive affirmative consent
> and otherwise destroy all state). No amount of regular re-attestation
> can replace this kind of guarantee.
> 
> 
> 
> 
> S 3.9
> 
> >    The solution must not degrade the privacy of a standard secure
> >    connection (e.g., the (D)TLS connection).  Evidence can contain
> >    highly specific, unique information about a device's hardware and
> >    software, which could be used as an advanced tracking mechanism,
> >    following a user across different connections and services.  The
> >    design must consider how to minimize this leakage, especially when a
> >    third-party Verifier is involved in the protocol exchange.
> 
> 
> This seems like it's in direct conflict with the requirement to
> bind to the machine identifier in S 4.2.
> 
> S 4.1.
> 
> >    An operator sends a critical command to a remote system (e.g., an
> >    industrial controller, a financial transaction processor).
> > 
> >    *  Requirement: The system must provide fresh Evidence to the
> >       operator to prove its integrity before the command is dispatched.
> >       This prevents commands from being executed on a compromised
> >       system.
> 
> I don't understand this case. If the system is compromised it can do
> anything it wants, including executing commands. Is the idea that the
> command is secret? That the operator wants to know if the command was
> actually executed?
> 
> 
> S 4.2.2
> 
> >    Distributed parties collaboratively compute a function (e.g., train a
> >    machine learning model) without sharing their local data.
> > 
> >    *  Requirement: The central aggregator, as well as each participating
> >       client, must be able to mutually attest to ensure all parties are
> >       running the correct, untampered MPC algorithm in a trusted
> >       environment.
> 
> Why? Is this about the integrity of the result? If so, I would
> observe that zero-knowedge proofs are a much stronger way
> of achieving this objectives.
> 
> 
> S 4.3.1.  Network Infrastructure Integrity
> 
> >    *  Requirement: The network orchestrator must verify the device's
> >       integrity (e.g., secure boot enabled, running signed OS and
> >       firmware) before allowing it to join the network and receive
> >       policy.  This prevents a compromised router from misdirecting
> >       traffic or a malicious VNF from inspecting sensitive packets.
> 
> I don't see how this works. As I understand the description here, a
> new device joins the network and you form a TLS connection to that
> device and require that it attest to its integrity, after which you
> let it handle traffic. However, I don't see what stops an attacker
> from adding a compromised device in between the network and a
> non-compromised device, and forwarding the TLS traffic, but then
> otherwise misbehaving. In order to prevent this, all network traffic
> that is to be be handled by the device has to be sent over the TLS
> channel, which is a highly unusual configuration.
> 
> S 4.3.2.
> 
> >    *  Requirement: The network orchestrator must verify the device's
> >       integrity (e.g., secure boot enabled, running signed OS and
> >       firmware) before allowing it to join the network and receive
> >       policy.  This prevents a compromised router from misdirecting
> >       traffic or a malicious VNF from inspecting sensitive packets.
> 
> I don't understand what "connecting to a compromised interface that
> could manipulate the device means". How does that work? As for "could
> steal credentials", the better approach is to use public-key based
> client authentication, thus removing the threat of bearer credentials.
> 
> 
> 
> S 4.5.
> 
> >    In this scenario, the peer acting as the Relying Party requires
> >    additional assurance that the private key associated with the end-
> >    entity certificate used to authenticate the TLS connection is
> >    generated, stored, and used within an attested cryptographic module.
> 
> This entire use case seems conclusory. Why does the TLS endpoint
> need this?
> 
> >    The approach described in [I-D.draft-ietf-rats-pkix-key-attestation]
> >    addresses this use case partially by providing attestation of the
> >    cryptographic module and associated private key at certificate
> >    issuance time, reflecting their state when the certificate is
> >    enrolled.  This model does not provide guarantees about the continued
> >    state of the module at connection establishment or during the
> >    lifetime of the TLS session.
> 
> I don't understand the security logic: given the original assertions
> listed above, which more or less amount to the key not available
> outside the module, what does fresh authentication get you? In
> order for these guarantees to be violated, you would presumably
> need to break whatever tamper resistance is in the module, but
> then you would also quite likely be able to forge whatever Evidence
> you need.what am I missing?
> 
> 
> S 5.
> 
> >    However, any solution must
> >    address the following high-level considerations:
> > 
> >    ...
> > 
> >    *  Evidence Semantics: This document does not define attestation
> >       appraisal policies.  However, a Relying Party must be careful when
> >       interpreting Attestation Results.  A "valid" attestation only
> >       means the Evidence is authentic and correctly signed; it does not
> >       automatically mean the underlying system is "secure".  The Relying
> >       Party must have a clear policy for what measurements, software
> >       versions, and security configurations are acceptable.
> 
> This actually seems like a dislaimer of solving this problem, not
> a requirement to address

issues.title: Clarify key non-exportability to allow secure replication/migration
issues.author: yaronf
issues.body:
Section 4.5 requires Evidence that the TLS private key:

> is generated and stored within a specific cryptographic module or secure element

and

> is protected against export or software extraction

Is the intention to require that a private key can never leave the particular cryptographic module in which it was generated?

That seems too restrictive for clustered/HA TLS deployments. For example, HSM clusters commonly support secure replication of a TLS private key between HSMs, while ensuring that the key is never exposed in plaintext outside the trusted cryptographic boundary. A similar requirement may arise when a confidential workload is migrated between platforms (cf. Section 4.6).

I think the desired security property is instead that the private key cannot be extracted into an untrusted environment. Secure transfer or replication directly between attested/trusted cryptographic environments should not necessarily violate that property.

Could Section 4.5 distinguish **software/plaintext extraction** from **secure key migration or replication between qualifying trusted environments**?

For example, the requirements might say that the key:

* is generated within, or securely provisioned into, an attested cryptographic module or secure element;
* is stored and used only within cryptographic environments satisfying the applicable security policy; and
* is protected against disclosure outside those environments, including extraction into ordinary software.

A deployment could still impose the stronger policy that a particular key is non-migratable and remains bound to one physical module, but that would not be a fundamental requirement of the SEAT use case.

(While I believe the specific wire-format fields belong to the solution definition rather than the use case, the intention here is to ensure freshness and channel binding.)

There are two primary drivers for this requirement:
⦁	High-impact operations often happen in the middle of complex, stateful application flows (e.g., a multi-turn AI agent conversation). Forcing a full TLS handshake often implies tearing down the underlying transport, which can disrupt application context/buffers. We need to verify security posture without dropping the application state.
⦁	If an application needs to verify integrity before every sensitive micro-transaction, a lightweight re-attestation token within the existing tunnel is significantly more performant than renegotiating the entire connection.

comments.author: ionut-arm
comments.body:
> What exactly is the difference between "threat model" and "attacker model?"

An attacker model describes the types of attacks one might expect for some given design or system: what capabilities, resources, and access the attackers might have, what they're trying to achieve...

The threat model is significantly wider in scope and covers a more concrete system: it shows what assets there are to protect, what attackers can do, what mitigations are (or can be) deployed, likelihood of attacks or issues, etc. The attacker model is one of the inputs to that. It's also more concrete, as it needs a more concrete description of the deployed system.

For an IETF protocol specification, a deployment-independent attacker model may be more useful than a comprehensive deployment-specific threat model. It establishes the adversary capabilities and security assumptions that apply across anticipated use-cases, while individual deployments can extend it with threats arising from their architecture, trust relationships, and operational environment.

"Remote attestation bound to the authenticated TLS connection provides an

comments.body:
### Unauthorized System Hosting of Valid Credentials

**Attacker capabilities:** A malicious peer possesses a valid, CA-endorsed authentication private key for an authorized peer identity and controls an endorsed Target Environment capable of producing authentic, fresh Evidence.

**Targeted assurance:** The Relying Party verifies that the specific Target Environment is authorized to execute operations under the authenticated peer identity, preventing communication with an unauthorized system.

**Preconditions and attack:** The Relying Party validates identity credentials and platform Evidence independently. The attacker hosts the valid key inside an unapproved confidential workload, completes the cryptographic transcript binding, and establishes the TLS connection. When the Relying Party's policy checks pass in isolation, it authorizes the session.

**Why validation succeeds:** TLS proof of possession and platform Evidence verify against their respective independent trust roots, and the connection binder confirms channel co-location. Validation succeeds because neither root evaluates the other's domain, and the Relying Party lacks a policy rule linking them. Cryptographic channel binding alone is insufficient to establish that an attested environment is an authorized system for a given identity.

**Required invariant:** To prevent communication with an unauthorized system,
compound authentication requires joint evaluation of the peer identity and
platform measurements.

I think this is basically identical to the `Key Substitution` attack described above, but your focus seems to be on how the RP makes decisions about which attesting platform is (or is not) legitimate, i.e. what the appraisal policy looks like for the RP.

My problem with this framing is in the `Required invariant` - we can't use it as a basis for a new property in this document, because it cannot be fulfilled / resolved by the aTLS protocol directly. (The goal of this section is to describe the attacks that _can_ be mitigated by the protocol.) At best, solution documents can say something along the lines of "the RP must properly authenticate the entity from which it receives appraisal policies", but this text would be identical to all solutions. Hence, I think it is better suited in an architecture document for SEAT.

> 
> [...] > At best, solution documents can say something along the lines of "the RP must properly authenticate the entity from which it receives appraisal policies",

This risk about _not_ doing the check in the first place, and I am trying to establish the boundary of what compound authentication with aTLS means in practice. 

My concern is that it was not initially obvious to me that these two checks (even when completely healthy) happen in isolated-silos, and someone may choose to forgo any configuration in the first place intended to tie the two disparate checks together. This may happen because one may assume erroneously (via either timing window) that the protocol achieves this cross-referencing for them automatically through the cryptography or inherent nature of the composed protocol design.
